analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal to gouge prices on gasoline, oil, and natural gas during declared energy emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 123 cosponsors after the 2005 hurricanes, never got a vote: it sat in House subcommittees until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the President declare a federal energy emergency when fuel supplies are disrupted or prices show unusual spikes. During such an emergency, selling gasoline, oil, natural gas, or petroleum products at unconscionably excessive prices would be unlawful, with civil fines up to triple the excess profits and criminal fines up to $100 million for corporations. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the ban, wholesale price information would have to be made public, and all fines collected would go into a fund for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which helps low-income households pay heating and cooling bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers in regions hit by fuel shortages or price spikes, since price gouging during declared emergencies would carry fines and even criminal penalties. Low-income households would also benefit indirectly, because every fine collected would be deposited into a trust fund supporting LIHEAP energy bill assistance. Honest fuel sellers would gain from public wholesale price data that makes collusion harder.

how_it_helps.text: During a declared energy emergency, it becomes unlawful to charge unconscionably excessive prices for gasoline, oil, natural gas, and petroleum products, with a gross disparity from pre-emergency prices as one test [S3].
Civil penalties reach three times the excess profits or $3 million per violation, and corporations can face criminal fines up to $100 million, with individuals facing up to 10 years in prison [S3].
The FTC must prioritize enforcement against companies with more than $500 million in annual US fuel sales, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents at the retail level [S3].
All fines and penalties go into a Consumer Relief Trust Fund used to assist low-income households through the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program [S3].
The FTC would facilitate price transparency in wholesale crude oil and petroleum markets, disseminating price and availability information to the public to discourage manipulation and collusion [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers, refiners, wholesalers, and retailers who raise prices unreasonably during an emergency would pay civil fines up to triple their excess profits and potentially criminal fines up to $100 million per violation. The broader fuel industry would also bear new reporting duties for wholesale price transparency, and compliance and litigation costs would ultimately flow through to fuel prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil producers, refiners, and fuel sellers

drawbacks.text: Price caps during shortages can backfire: if sellers cannot raise prices when supply is scarce, fuel may sell out quickly, lines and hoarding can follow, and suppliers have less incentive to rush fuel into the affected region. The bill tries to soften this by letting sellers show their higher price reflected genuine cost increases they could not control [S3].

The 'unconscionably excessive' standard is vague, and the emergency trigger includes 'significant pricing anomalies' rather than only physical shortages, so a President could potentially invoke emergency pricing limits during ordinary price run-ups, chilling legitimate price changes [S3].

The FTC and courts would bear the cost of building enforcement machinery and new wholesale price-reporting rules within 180 days of enactment, and those administrative costs are appropriations the bill merely authorizes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and widely felt harm — fuel prices spiking when supply is disrupted — and includes genuine safeguards for sellers whose higher prices reflect real costs. Its biggest weakness is economic: caps during scarcity can worsen shortages if they suppress the price signals that draw in supply, and the vague standards give both enforcers and the President wide discretion. On balance it is a consumer-protection bill whose costs fall mainly on companies that profit from emergency run-ups, with the design risk that it occasionally constrains legitimate pricing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with 123 cosponsors and referred to two House committees, which sent it to subcommittees; no committee ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak and 33 other House members introduced the bill on September 28, 2005 [S3].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee [S1].
The bill drew 123 cosponsors — 122 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].

On October 17, 2005 it was referred to the Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection Subcommittee, and on November 7, 2005 to the Education Reform Subcommittee; neither took further action on the bill [S5].
The sponsor made introductory remarks on the House floor several more times through July 2006, but the bill never advanced to a committee vote or floor action [S5].
The 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007, and the bill received no vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, refiners, and fuel wholesalers and retailers came out ahead: they faced no federal price-gouging penalties, no market-manipulation rules, and no new wholesale price transparency requirements. Consumers gained nothing from a bill that 123 members supported but that never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would expose large producers and refiners to civil fines up to triple excess profits and criminal fines up to $100 million for unconscionable pricing, false price reports, or wholesale market manipulation during declared emergencies. Blocking the bill preserved their freedom to price freely during supply disruptions.

Wholesalers would face manipulation rules and mandatory public price reporting, while retailers could be sued by state attorneys general for emergency price gouging. Without the bill, retail price spikes during hurricanes and other disruptions carried no new federal penalty.

industries.industry: Low-income energy assistance (LIHEAP) programs and the households they serve
industries.note: The bill would have funded LIHEAP through fines collected under the act, adding resources for low-income heating and cooling help. Because the bill died, that funding stream never materialized.
